I played a game of chess with my uncle.
For lunch, my dad cooked kabsa for the whole family.
After lunch I relaxed on the sofa with a cold drink.

dialogue.t: How was your weekend?
It was quiet. We stayed at home.
What happened on Friday?
We watched a film about the ocean.
And on Saturday?
My dad cooked kabsa, and I played a game of chess.

grammar.title: Past simple: regular verbs + -ed
grammar.ar: للحديث عن شيء حدث وانتهى نضيف ed للفعل: play ← played، watch ← watched. الفعل نفسه لكل الأشخاص.
examples: I played a game with my sister.
We watched a film on Friday.
My mum cooked rice and chicken.

words.ex: Last Friday we visited my grandparents in Qassim.
Last weekend I visited my aunt and her new baby.
I helped my grandpa with his garden.
Grandma baked a date cake for us.
My mum and my aunt chatted for hours.
We laughed a lot at my uncle's funny jokes.

dialogue.t: What did you do last weekend?
We visited my grandparents on their farm.
What happened there?
I helped my grandpa with the palm trees.
And your grandma?
She baked a date cake, and we chatted in the garden.
That sounds lovely!

grammar.title: Spelling: -d, -ied and double letters
grammar.ar: إذا انتهى الفعل بـ e نضيف d فقط: bake ← baked. وإذا انتهى بحرف ساكن ثم y نحوّلها إلى ied: carry ← carried. وبعض الأفعال القصيرة نضاعف آخر حرف: chat ← chatted.
examples: Grandma baked a cake.
I carried the dates to the car.
We chatted in the garden.

words.ex: Yesterday at school we started a new science project.
Our class started a project about the moon.
In art class Reem painted a picture of the desert at sunset.
We practised our song for the school show.
I finished my maths homework in the library.
At break we chatted about the football match.

dialogue.t: How was school yesterday?
Busy! We started a project about the planets.
What happened in art class?
I painted a picture of Saturn.
And in PE?
We practised for Sports Day.

grammar.title: Time words: yesterday, this morning, last …
grammar.ar: نستخدم كلمات الزمن مع الماضي: yesterday (أمس)، this morning (هذا الصباح)، last week (الأسبوع الماضي). نضعها في أول الجملة أو آخرها.
examples: Yesterday we practised for Sports Day.
I finished my project this morning.
Our class started a new book last week.

words.ex: Two days ago our team played against Class 5B.
Yesterday I watched a match between Al Hilal and Al Nassr.
Omar passed the ball to me, and I kicked it hard.
Salem scored a goal in the first five minutes.
He kicked hard but missed the goal.
Everyone cheered when the match ended.

dialogue.t: How was the match?
Great! Two days ago we played against Class 5B.
What happened?
I passed the ball to Ali, but he missed.
Oh no!
Then he scored a goal, and everyone cheered!

grammar.title: Time words: ago and last
grammar.ar: نستخدم ago بعد المدة: two days ago (قبل يومين). ونستخدم last قبل الزمن: last Thursday (الخميس الماضي). لا نقول the last week.
examples: We played a match two days ago.
Last Thursday I scored a goal.
My team practised three weeks ago.

words.ex: I tidied my room before my cousins arrived.
After dinner, I washed the dishes with my sister.
I carried the shopping bags to the kitchen.
Faisal emptied the bin in the kitchen last night.
I helped my dad with the car.
We cleaned the car. After that, we watched TV.

dialogue.t: Was your weekend busy?
Yes! Our aunts visited us, so I helped my mum.
What did you do?
First, I tidied my room.
And after that?
After that, I washed the dishes and carried the coffee.

grammar.title: First … After that …
grammar.ar: لترتيب الأحداث نستخدم First (أولاً) ثم After that (بعد ذلك). نضع فاصلة بعدهما.
examples: First, I tidied my room.
After that, I emptied the bin.
First, we cooked lunch. After that, we washed the dishes.

words.ex: First, we visited my uncle.
Then we walked in the park.
After that, my family cooked dinner together.
Finally, I had a shower and relaxed.
We really enjoyed the cool evening in the park.
On Saturday we visited the new science museum.

dialogue.t: Tell me about your weekend.
First, we stayed at home and played board games.
And then?
Then the rain stopped, and we walked in the park.
What about Saturday?
We visited my aunt. Finally, we watched the stars. I really enjoyed it!

grammar.title: Telling a story in order
grammar.ar: نحكي القصة بالترتيب: First (أولاً) ← Then (ثم) ← After that (بعد ذلك) ← Finally (أخيراً)، مع أفعال ماضية.
examples: First, we visited my aunt.
Then we walked to the park. After that, we played football.
Finally, we returned home and relaxed.

words.ex: Last summer we went to the beach in Jeddah.
I swam in the sea for an hour.
We had a picnic on the beach with sandwiches and juice.
My sister and I built a sandcastle near the water.
On the beach I found a beautiful white shell.
We came back home at nine o'clock, very tired.

dialogue.t: Where did you go last weekend?
We went to the beach in Jeddah.
Did you swim in the sea?
Yes, I did. The water was warm.
Did you build a sandcastle?
Yes! My sister and I built a huge one.

grammar.title: Past simple: irregular verbs
grammar.ar: بعض الأفعال لا نضيف لها ed بل تتغيّر كلها في الماضي، ونحفظها: go ← went، swim ← swam، build ← built، find ← found، come ← came.
examples: We went to the beach.
I swam in the sea.
My brother found a shell.

words.ex: Last winter we went to the desert near Riyadh.
My uncle drove us to the sand dunes.
My little brother rode a camel for the first time.
We made a campfire and cooked dinner on it.
At night we saw hundreds of stars.
We slept in a big tent near the sand dunes.

dialogue.t: Did you go camping last weekend?
Yes, I did. We went to the desert.
What did you do there?
I rode a camel, and we made a campfire.
Where did you sleep?
We slept in a tent and saw hundreds of stars.

grammar.title: Did you …? Yes, I did. / No, I didn't.
grammar.ar: للسؤال عن الماضي: Did + الفاعل + الفعل في صورته الأساسية. نقول Did you ride? ولا نقول Did you rode? والجواب القصير: Yes, I did. / No, I didn't.
examples: Did you ride a camel? — Yes, I did.
Did you sleep in a tent? — No, I didn't.
Did your dad drive? — Yes, he did.

words.ex: At the museum we saw an old map of Arabia.
I took photos of the old swords.
We learnt about the history of Riyadh.
Our guide showed us a big rock from space.
We saw ancient writing on a big stone.
At the museum shop I bought a souvenir for my sister.

dialogue.t: What did you see at the museum?
We saw ancient writing on big stones.
Did you take photos?
Yes, lots! I took photos of the old swords.
What did you buy?
I bought a souvenir for my brother.

grammar.title: What / Where did …?
grammar.ar: نضع كلمة السؤال قبل did: What did you see? Where did you go? والفعل بعد did يبقى في صورته الأساسية (see وليس saw).
examples: What did you see? — We saw old maps.
Where did you buy it? — At the museum shop.
What did you learn about? — The history of Riyadh.

words.ex: Last spring we flew from Riyadh to AlUla.
We went to Abha by car. It took ten hours.
We stayed at a hotel in the desert for three nights.
On the trip we met a family from Italy.
The view from the mountain was amazing.
In AlUla I took photos of the huge rocks.

dialogue.t: How did you get to AlUla?
We flew from Jeddah.
Where did you stay?
We stayed at a small hotel for three nights.
Who did you meet there?
We met a family from Spain.

grammar.title: How / Who / How long …?
grammar.ar: How did you get there? للسؤال عن وسيلة السفر، وWho did you meet? للسؤال عن الأشخاص، وHow long did you stay? للسؤال عن المدة.
examples: How did you get there? — By plane.
Who did you meet? — A family from Spain.
How long did you stay? — Three nights.

words.ex: We had fun at Boulevard World last night.
My favourite ride was the big wheel.
We got tickets for the show online.
For dinner we ate burgers and fresh juice.
The park was very crowded on Thursday night.
At the shop I bought a toy falcon.

dialogue.t: Did you go to Riyadh Season?
Yes, we went on Thursday night.
Was it crowded?
Very crowded, but we had fun!
What did you eat?
We ate noodles and ice cream.

grammar.title: Was it …? / Were they …?
grammar.ar: للسؤال عن الوصف في الماضي نستخدم Was / Were بدون did: Was it crowded? Were the rides fun? والجواب: Yes, it was. / No, they weren't.
examples: Was it crowded? — Yes, it was.
Were the rides fun? — Yes, they were.
Was the food good? — No, it wasn't.

words.ex: Where did you go last summer? — To Abha.
How did you get to Abha? — By car.
Who did you go to the beach with? — My cousins.
What did you do in Jeddah? — We swam and fished.
We had fun when we rode the cable car.
We came back from Abha after a week.

dialogue.t: Where did you go in the holidays?
I went to Abha.
How did you get there?
By car, with my family.
What did you do there?
We rode the cable car and had a picnic. We had fun!

grammar.title: Question words: Where, How, Who, What, When
grammar.ar: مراجعة كلمات السؤال في الماضي: كلمة السؤال + did + الفاعل + الفعل الأساسي. Where (أين) – How (كيف) – Who (من) – What (ماذا) – When (متى).
examples: Where did you go? — To Abha.
When did you come back? — After a week.
Who did you go with? — With my family.

words.ex: A cheetah is faster than a horse.
An elephant is stronger than a lion.
A whale is heavier than an elephant.
A shark is more dangerous than a dolphin.
The peregrine falcon is the fastest bird in the world.
My grandpa has a falcon called Saqr.

dialogue.t: Which is faster, a cheetah or a horse?
A cheetah is faster than a horse.
What's the fastest animal in the world?
The falcon!
Which is stronger, a lion or an elephant?
An elephant is stronger than a lion, and heavier too.

grammar.title: Comparatives: -er than
grammar.ar: للمقارنة بين شيئين نضيف er للصفة القصيرة ثم than: fast ← faster than، strong ← stronger than. وإذا انتهت الصفة بـ y نحوّلها إلى ier: heavy ← heavier.
examples: A cheetah is faster than a horse.
An elephant is stronger than a lion.
A whale is heavier than an elephant.

words.ex: Riyadh is bigger than Abha.
In summer, Riyadh is hotter than Taif.
The city centre is busier than our street.
I think Abha is more beautiful than Riyadh in summer.
Riyadh is the biggest city in Saudi Arabia.
The fastest way to get from Makkah to Madinah is by train.

dialogue.t: Is Riyadh the biggest city in Saudi Arabia?
Yes. It's bigger than Jeddah and busier too.
Which city is cooler in summer?
Abha. It's cooler than Riyadh.
What's the fastest way to get there?
By plane.

grammar.title: Spelling: bigger, hotter, busier
grammar.ar: إذا كانت الصفة قصيرة وتنتهي بحرف علّة واحد ثم حرف ساكن نضاعف الحرف الأخير: big ← bigger، hot ← hotter. وإذا انتهت بـ y نحوّلها إلى ier: busy ← busier.
examples: Riyadh is bigger than Abha.
July is hotter than March.
The mall is busier than the park.

words.ex: I think football is more exciting than golf.
Swimming is easier than running for me.
Tennis is harder than badminton because the ball is fast.
I'm better at volleyball than basketball.
The most popular sport at my school is football.
Basketball is faster than volleyball.

dialogue.t: What about football for Sports Day?
It's the most popular sport, but it's long.
Basketball is more exciting than football.
Yes, but it's harder.
Volleyball is easier than basketball.
Good! I'm better at volleyball.

grammar.title: more … than / better than
grammar.ar: مع الصفات الطويلة نستخدم more … than: exciting ← more exciting than. والصفة good لها شكل خاص: good ← better، وbad ← worse.
examples: Football is more exciting than golf.
I'm better at swimming than running.
My first game was worse than my second game.

words.ex: The Burj Khalifa is taller than the Kingdom Centre.
The Burj Khalifa is the tallest building in the world.
Masmak Fort is older than the Kingdom Centre.
The most famous building in Paris is the Eiffel Tower.
From the top of the tower, you can see the whole city.
The biggest building I visited was a huge mall in Riyadh.

dialogue.t: Is the Kingdom Centre very tall?
Yes, but the Burj Khalifa is taller.
Is it the tallest building in the world?
Yes, it is!
Which is older, Masmak Fort or the Kingdom Centre?
Masmak Fort is older.

grammar.title: Superlatives: the -est / the most …
grammar.ar: للمقارنة بين أكثر من شيئين نستخدم صيغة التفضيل مع the: tall ← the tallest، old ← the oldest، famous ← the most famous.
examples: The Burj Khalifa is the tallest building in the world.
The pyramids are the oldest buildings on our list.
The Eiffel Tower is the most famous building in Paris.

words.ex: The puzzle is cheaper than the doll.
The red bike is more expensive than the blue one.
This school bag is lighter than my old one.
The old phone is worse than the new one because the battery is weak.
The cheapest bike in the shop is 400 riyals.
The blue bike is better than the green one because it has good brakes.

dialogue.t: This red bike is lighter than my old one.
Yes, but it's more expensive than the blue one.
Which one is the cheapest?
The green one, but its brakes are worse.
The blue one is better than the green one.
And it's cheaper than the red one!

grammar.title: good – better – the best / bad – worse – the worst
grammar.ar: بعض الصفات لها أشكال خاصة: good ← better ← the best، وbad ← worse ← the worst. لا نقول gooder أو badder.
examples: The blue bike is better than the green one.
This is the best bike in the shop.
The weather today is worse than yesterday.

words.ex: The best day this year was Sports Day.
The worst day of my week is Monday because I have two tests.
The funniest person in my family is my uncle Saad.
The most interesting lesson this year was about volcanoes.
The most popular game in our class is football.
The longest trip I took was to Tabuk by car.

dialogue.t: Who's the funniest person in the class?
Khalid! His jokes are the funniest.
What was the most interesting trip?
The museum trip. It was more interesting than the zoo trip.
And the worst thing this year?
The longest maths test!

grammar.title: Comparatives and superlatives together
grammar.ar: نستخدم المقارنة (er / more) بين شيئين، والتفضيل (the -est / the most) بين ثلاثة أشياء أو أكثر.
examples: Omar is funny. Khalid is funnier. Salem is the funniest.
This test is long. That test is longer. The maths test is the longest.
Art is interesting. Science is more interesting. The museum trip was the most interesting.

words.ex: Eggs, bread and fruit are a healthy breakfast.
You shouldn't skip breakfast before school.
My favourite fresh fruit is mango.
Fizzy drinks are very sugary.
I feel full of energy after a good breakfast.
You should eat an egg and some fruit for breakfast.

dialogue.t: You look tired. Are you OK?
I skipped breakfast this morning.
You shouldn't skip breakfast.
I only had a chocolate bar.
That's very sugary. You should eat eggs and fresh fruit.
OK, thanks!

grammar.title: should / shouldn't
grammar.ar: نستخدم should + الفعل الأساسي لنعطي نصيحة (من الأفضل أن)، وshouldn't لنقول إن الشيء ليس فكرة جيدة. لا نضع to بعد should.
examples: You should eat fresh fruit.
You shouldn't skip breakfast.
He should drink milk, not fizzy drinks.

words.ex: What's the matter, Omar? You look sad.
When I have a cold, I stay at home and rest.
For a sore throat, you should drink warm water with honey.
You should get some rest and stay in bed.
My favourite warm drink is ginger tea.
You should see a doctor because you have a high temperature.

dialogue.t: What's the matter?
I've got a cold and a sore throat.
You should get some rest.
What should I drink?
You should have a warm drink, like tea with honey.
Thanks!

grammar.title: What's the matter? + advice
grammar.ar: نسأل عن المشكلة بـ What's the matter? والجواب I've got a cold / a sore throat. ثم نعطي النصيحة بـ You should أو You shouldn't.
examples: What's the matter? — I've got a cold.
You should get some rest.
You shouldn't go out in the rain.

words.ex: On school nights, I go to bed early, at nine o'clock.
At the weekend I sometimes stay up late and watch a film.
My screen time every day is about two hours.
I feel tired when I stay up late.
After a good night's sleep, I feel happy and ready for school.
After school, I get some rest by reading on the sofa.

dialogue.t: Why are you so tired?
I stayed up late. I played games until midnight.
You shouldn't stay up late on school nights.
Should I use my tablet in bed?
No, you shouldn't. You should read a book.
OK. Tonight I can go to bed early.

grammar.title: Should I …? Yes, you should. / No, you shouldn't.
grammar.ar: لطلب النصيحة نسأل: Should I + الفعل الأساسي؟ والجواب القصير: Yes, you should. / No, you shouldn't.
examples: Should I go to bed early? — Yes, you should.
Should I use my phone in bed? — No, you shouldn't.
Should we turn off the TV? — Yes, you should.

words.ex: On hot days, I drink plenty of water when I play outside.
I feel thirsty after football practice.
We had lunch in the shade of a big tree.
You should wear a cap when you walk in the sun.
You should put on sun cream before you go to the beach.
On hot days, cold water is better than sugary drinks.

dialogue.t: Let's play football now!
It's midday. We shouldn't play outside now.
When should we play?
In the evening. And you should wear a cap.
What should I take?
You should take plenty of water.

grammar.title: When / What should I …?
grammar.ar: لطلب النصيحة يمكن أن نبدأ بكلمة سؤال: When should we play? What should I take? والفعل بعد should يبقى في صورته الأساسية.
examples: When should we play? — In the evening.
What should I take? — Water and a cap.
Where should we sit? — In the shade.

words.ex: I exercise by riding my bike every afternoon.
Before a football match, you should warm up.
After running, I stretch my legs.
I'm out of breath after I run up the stairs.
When I'm tired, I take a break and drink some water.
After exercise, I feel full of energy and happy.

dialogue.t: I want to win the race. What should I do?
You should exercise every day.
Should I run very fast?
No, you shouldn't. Always warm up first.
What should I do when I'm out of breath?
You should take a break and drink some water.

grammar.title: should always / should never
grammar.ar: يمكن أن نضع always (دائماً) أو never (أبداً) بعد should: You should always warm up. You should never run after a big meal.
examples: You should always warm up first.
You should never exercise without water.
You should stretch after running.

words.ex: My best tip for a healthy life is to sleep well.
One of my healthy habits is walking to school.
I sometimes eat junk food when we go to the cinema.
To stay fit, I swim twice a week.
You should drink plenty of water when it's hot.
You should go to bed early before a big test.

dialogue.t: What's our first tip?
You should drink plenty of water.
And number two?
You shouldn't eat too much junk food.
What about sleep?
You should go to bed early on school nights.
Great poster!

grammar.title: Giving tips with reasons
grammar.ar: نبدأ كل نصيحة بـ You should أو You shouldn't + الفعل الأساسي، ونضيف السبب بـ because.
examples: You should drink plenty of water because it keeps you cool.
You shouldn't eat too much junk food because it isn't healthy.
You should exercise every day because it keeps you fit.

pages.text: Faisal and his grandfather drove to a quiet beach by the Red Sea. They put up their tent near the soft sand. "Tonight, we will sleep under the stars," Grandfather said with a smile.
After dinner, Faisal walked along the beach with a torch. Suddenly, something moved near his foot. It was a tiny turtle, smaller than his hand! Then he saw another one, and another.

But the baby turtles were walking away from the sea, towards the bright lights of a small café. "Why are they going the wrong way?" Faisal asked. "Baby turtles follow the brightest light," Grandfather explained. "It is usually the moon on the water."
"The café is brighter than the moon!" Faisal said. "We must help them." He switched off his torch, and Grandfather turned off the car lights. But the café lights were still shining.

Faisal ran to the café as fast as he could. "Excuse me, sir," he said to the owner. "Can you please turn off your lights for a few minutes? Baby turtles are lost on the beach." The man looked surprised, but he quickly pressed a switch.
Now the beach was dark, and the silver moon shone on the sea. Slowly, the little turtles turned around. One by one, they crawled down to the waves and swam away. Faisal counted twenty-three turtles!

The next morning, Faisal and the café owner made a sign: "Turtle Beach – Please keep lights off at night." "One day, those turtles will come back here to lay their eggs," Grandfather said. Faisal looked at the blue sea and felt very proud.

pages.text: Yousef wanted to win the school food fair. "What can we cook, Grandma?" he asked. Grandma smiled. "We're going to make kleeja, my special date cookies."
In the kitchen, they mixed flour, butter and cardamom. The house smelled wonderful. Then Grandma's phone rang, and she went to the living room. "Don't touch anything!" she called.
But little Huda wanted to help. She took a white jar and put three big spoons into the bowl. "More sugar makes it sweeter!" she said happily. Nobody saw the label on the jar. It said SALT.
Later, Yousef tasted the dough. "Yuck! It's so salty!" he shouted. Huda started to cry. The fair was tomorrow, and there were no more dates in the house.

Grandma looked at the bowl and laughed. "Don't worry. A good cook can fix a mistake," she said. She took cheese from the fridge and za'atar from the cupboard. "Today, our kleeja is going to be different."

The next day, the tables at the fair were full of cakes, chocolate and biscuits. The judges tried them all. "Too much sugar!" one judge whispered. Then she bit into Yousef's warm cheese cookie, and her eyes opened wide.
Yousef won the prize for the Most Surprising Dish! Everyone wanted the recipe. "It was a team idea," Yousef said, and he gave the prize to Huda. "She's our secret chef!"

stories.title: The Night the Lights Went Out

pages.text: Lina loved sounds. She heard music everywhere: in the bubbling coffee pot, in the rain on the window, and in her little brother's spoon on his plate. She kept a notebook and wrote down all her favourite sounds.

One morning, Ms Huda said, "Our class is going to play music for our families next Thursday!" Everyone was excited, but Lina was worried. "I can't play the keyboard or the drum," she said quietly. "Then you can help me with the lights," Ms Huda said with a smile.

On Thursday evening, the school hall was full of mothers, fathers and grandparents. Hamad started the first song on the electric keyboard, and the music was loud and bright. Suddenly, there was a strange noise, and all the lights went out.
The hall was dark and very quiet. The keyboard was silent too, because there was no electricity. A baby started to cry, and Hamad whispered, "What are we going to do now?"
Lina remembered her notebook of sounds. She turned on the torch on Ms Huda's phone and tapped two pencils on a table: tap, tap, tap-tap-tap. "Everyone, copy me!" she called.

First the children clapped, and then the parents joined in. Some people tapped their feet, and some knocked gently on their chairs. Soon the whole dark hall was full of music, and the baby stopped crying and laughed.

When the lights came back ten minutes later, everyone cheered. The next day, Ms Huda gave Lina a real drum. "You don't need electricity to make music," she said. "You only need good ears and a brave heart."

stories.title: The Case of the Missing Dates

pages.text: Layla wanted to be a detective. She always carried a small notebook and a magnifying glass in her bag. One morning, Grandma came into the kitchen with an empty plate. "My dates are gone again!" she said.

Every evening, Grandma put a plate of fresh dates on the table in the garden for her guests. But every morning, some of the dates were missing. "Who is taking them?" asked Omar, Layla's little brother. "Let's find out," Layla said, and she opened her notebook.

First, Layla looked for clues. Under the table, she found four date stones and some tiny footprints in the sand. "These aren't Omar's footprints," she said. "They are too small, and they only have three thin toes!"
Omar laughed. "Maybe it's a very small thief with no shoes!" But Layla was thinking hard. Then she found a black and brown feather on the garden wall.
The next day, Layla and Omar woke up before sunrise. They hid behind the kitchen window and watched the table quietly. Soon they heard a loud, happy noise above the garden.

Two brown birds with yellow eyes flew down to the table. Each bird took a date and flew up to the top of the palm tree. Layla looked through her magnifying glass and saw a nest with three hungry baby birds inside!

"Case closed!" Layla said proudly at breakfast. Grandma smiled and put a small plate of dates near the palm tree for the birds. Then she covered the guests' dates with a net. "Now everyone in this garden can enjoy a good breakfast," she said.

pages.text: Yousef loved superheroes. Every night, he drew comics about Captain Falcon, a hero who could fly faster than a plane. "I wish I had a superpower," he told his grandfather. Grandpa smiled and said, "Maybe you already have one."

On Friday evening, the family went to the old market. It was full of people, bright lights and the smell of spices. Yousef looked at everything carefully, like he always did before he drew something. He saw a small boy in a red cap. The boy was holding a toy camel and walking next to a woman with a green bag.

Later, near the perfume shop, Yousef heard someone crying. It was the boy in the red cap, but now he was alone. "I can't find my mum!" he cried. Yousef's heart was beating fast, but he knelt down and said, "Don't worry. I'll help you."

Yousef closed his eyes and remembered. Before, the boy's mother was buying dates at the shop next to the fountain. Her bag was green with yellow flowers on it. "Grandpa, follow me!" Yousef said, and they walked quickly through the busy market.
At the date shop, a woman was looking around. She looked very worried. In her hand, she held a green bag with yellow flowers. "Mama!" shouted the boy, and he ran into her arms.
The mother thanked Yousef again and again. "You are a real hero," she said. Yousef looked down at his shoes. "But I can't fly, and I don't have a cape."

Grandpa put his hand on Yousef's shoulder. "You noticed small things, and you were brave and kind. That is your superpower." That night, Yousef started a new comic. His new hero was called Captain Eyes.

stories.title: The Shoe Thief of the Desert

pages.text: Every winter, Faisal's family went camping in the desert. This year, Grandpa came too. They drove for two hours until they could see only red sand and a big blue sky.

Dad and Faisal put up the tent, and Noura helped Mum with the fire. At night, Grandpa pointed at the sky. "Look, that bright star always shows the north," he said. "Our grandfathers used the stars like a map."
Later, everyone was sleeping when Faisal heard a strange noise outside. Scratch, scratch, scratch! He looked out quietly, but he couldn't see anything in the dark.
In the morning, one of his shoes was missing! "Who took my shoe?" Faisal shouted. Grandpa laughed and pointed at the small footprints next to the tent. "The desert can tell you," he said.
Faisal and Noura followed the footprints with Grandpa. They walked past dry bushes and over a small hill. Faisal had to wear his sandals, and the sand was getting hotter and hotter.

Behind a big rock, they found a hole. Next to it was Faisal's shoe, and two baby foxes were playing with it! Their mother watched them with her big ears. "Shh," whispered Grandpa. "Don't go closer. This is their home."

They waited quietly, and soon the foxes ran back into their hole. Faisal picked up his shoe slowly. It had a few small holes now, but he didn't mind. "Now you can read the desert too," Grandpa said with a smile.

pages.text: The big clock above our school door was very old. Every morning, it rang at seven o'clock, and every student ran to class. But one Sunday, it stopped. Nobody knew why.
"Sports Day is on Thursday," said our teacher, Mr. Khalid. "We need the clock to start the races!" The headteacher called a repair man, but he was busy until next month.
In our class there was a new boy called Omar. He was very quiet, and he always sat alone at break time. That day, I saw him looking up at the clock for a long time.
"My grandfather mends clocks," Omar said softly. "I help him in his shop every weekend." I was surprised. "Can you fix our clock?" I asked, and he answered, "Maybe, but I need to see inside it."

Mr. Khalid brought a ladder, and Omar climbed up carefully. He opened the back of the clock and looked inside with a small torch. "There's a bird's nest in here!" he laughed. "It's stopping the wheels."
Omar moved the nest gently into a tree, and he cleaned the wheels with a soft brush. Then he turned a tiny key. Tick, tock, tick, tock! All the students in the yard cheered.
On Thursday, the clock rang, and the first race began. Omar ran in it, and I ran next to him. We didn't win, but we laughed all the way to the finish line. Now Omar never sits alone at break time.

pages.text: It was a hot summer evening in Riyadh. Omar was playing a game on his tablet, Dad was watching football, and Mum was talking to Aunt Noura on the phone. Grandpa Saleh sat quietly in his chair with his coffee, and nobody was talking to him.
Suddenly, all the lights went out. The TV stopped, and the air conditioner was silent. "A power cut!" shouted Huda, Omar's little sister. "It's so dark!"
"It's too hot inside," said Dad. "Let's go up to the roof." They took a torch, some cold water and a plate of dates, and they climbed the stairs together.

On the roof, they heard a strange noise behind the water tank. Huda held Mum's hand tightly, and Omar was scared too. But he walked slowly towards the sound with the torch. Two shining green eyes looked back at him. It was only a small, thin cat!

Everyone laughed, and Huda gave the cat some water. Then Grandpa pointed at the sky. "Without the city lights, you can see the stars," he said. "When I was a boy in the desert, my father used these stars to find the way home."

Omar's tablet battery was empty, but he didn't care. He listened to Grandpa's stories about camels, long journeys and cold desert nights. Mum and Dad asked lots of questions, and Grandpa looked happier than ever.

After two hours, the lights came on again, but nobody wanted to go inside. "Grandpa," said Omar, "can we come up here every Thursday night?" Grandpa put his arm around him and smiled. "That's the best idea I've heard all year," he said.

pages.text: Omar got a small drone for his tenth birthday. It had a camera, and he could see its pictures on his tablet. "Be careful with it," said his father. "It isn't a toy."
On Friday, the family visited Grandpa's farm in the desert. Grandpa looked worried. "My falcon, Saqr, flew away this morning and didn't come back," he said.
Omar had an idea. "My drone can fly high and look for him!" he said. Grandpa laughed. "A machine can find a bird? Well, let's try."
The drone flew over the palm trees and the sand hills. Omar and his cousin Lama watched the screen carefully. Suddenly Lama shouted, "Stop! What's that brown shape near the old well?"
Omar moved the camera closer. It was Saqr! The falcon was sitting on the ground, and a long string was caught around his leg. He couldn't fly.
The family drove to the well quickly. Grandpa spoke softly to the bird and cut the string with his small knife. Saqr opened his wings and climbed onto Grandpa's arm.
That evening, everyone drank tea and ate dates outside under the stars. "I was wrong about your drone," Grandpa said with a smile. "Next time, can you teach me how to fly it?"

pages.text: This story happened in Cairo, about one thousand years ago. A boy called Yusuf lived near the busy market. Every afternoon, he carried bread and dates to an old scholar called Ibn al-Haytham.
The scholar's room was always dark. "Why do you close the windows, sir?" Yusuf asked. "Because I am studying light," the scholar answered with a smile.
One day, Ibn al-Haytham made a tiny hole in the wooden window. A thin line of sunlight came into the room. Suddenly, Yusuf saw colours on the white wall opposite.
"Look! It's the street!" Yusuf shouted. He could see a camel, a man with a basket and the green palm trees. But everything was upside down!
"Light travels in straight lines," the scholar explained. "It comes from the camel, goes through the hole and arrives on the wall. Our eyes work in the same way." Yusuf's mouth was wide open.
At that time, many people believed that light came out of our eyes. Ibn al-Haytham wanted to prove the truth, so he tested his ideas again and again. Then he wrote everything in a big book.
Yusuf never forgot that afternoon, and when he grew up, he became a scholar too. Today, cameras still use Ibn al-Haytham's simple idea: a small hole and a dark room.

pages.text: Every spring, Faisal visited his grandfather's farm in the desert. On Friday morning, the sky was clear and blue, and the sun was hot. Faisal looked at his phone. "The weather app says it will be sunny all day, Grandpa!"
Grandpa stood still and looked up at the sky for a long time. "The birds are flying low, and the wind smells of dust," he said quietly. "A sandstorm is coming this afternoon."

Faisal laughed. "But my phone is very clever, Grandpa!" Grandpa smiled. "Your phone is clever, but the sky is older." An hour later, Faisal saw something strange: a tall brown wall was moving across the desert towards them.
"Quick! Help me with the goats!" Grandpa shouted. Faisal ran after the goats and pushed them into the barn. Then he closed all the windows in the house while the wind got louder and louder.

Outside, everything was brown and dark, and they couldn't see the palm trees. Inside, Grandpa made sweet tea, and they listened to the wind. "My father learned about the weather from the clouds and the stars," Grandpa said. "He didn't need an app."

After two hours, the wind stopped. Then Faisal heard a soft sound on the roof. Rain! He ran outside and held out his hands, and the cool drops fell on his face. "Rain in the desert!" he shouted happily.

A week later, tiny green plants and yellow flowers covered the sand. Faisal opened his notebook and wrote: "Grandpa's weather rules: watch the birds, smell the wind, and look at the sky." Then he smiled at Grandpa. "Now I have two weather forecasts, and the best one isn't on my phone!"

pages.text: Yousef loved drawing, but he only used a black pencil. "Colours are too loud," he always said. One Sunday, his teacher, Mr. Khalid, had exciting news. "Our class is going to paint the long white wall next to the school gate!"

Everyone cheered, but Yousef was quiet. After school, he sat on the steps of his grandfather's old house. The big wooden door was covered in tiny triangles and circles. But the paint was pale and very old.

"Your grandmother painted this door fifty years ago," said Grandfather. "Every colour has a story. Red is for the desert at sunset, and green is for our palm trees." Yousef touched the small shapes, and for the first time, the colours didn't feel loud.

"Can we paint it again?" asked Yousef. They bought small pots of red, green, blue and yellow paint. All weekend, Yousef worked slowly and carefully with a thin brush. When he finished, the door looked bright and new.
On Monday, Yousef brought a photo of the door to school. "Can we paint a pattern like this on our wall?" he asked. Mr. Khalid smiled. "It's perfect, Yousef. You can be our pattern leader!"

For two weeks, the class measured, drew and painted. Yousef showed his friends how to draw triangles with a ruler. One day, Omar dropped a pot of yellow paint, and it made a big spot on the wall. Everybody laughed, and Yousef quickly turned the spot into a shining sun.

When the wall was finished, all the families came to see it. Grandfather stood in front of it for a long time. "Your grandmother would love this," he said quietly. That night, Yousef opened his pencil box and took out a red pencil.

pages.text: Faisal's grandfather had a small clock shop in old Jeddah. One afternoon, Grandpa went to pray at the mosque, and Faisal stayed in the shop alone. On the table, he saw an old silver watch with no numbers, only tiny stars.
"Never touch that watch," Grandpa always said. But Faisal was curious, so he turned the little wheel backwards. The shop started to spin, and all the clocks went quiet.
When Faisal opened his eyes, the street looked different. There were no cars, only camels and tall wooden houses with green windows. A boy ran past with a newspaper, and the date on it said 1965!

In front of the same shop, a thin boy was sitting on the ground with a broken clock. "It won't work, and my father says I'm not clever enough," he said sadly. Faisal sat down next to him. "Let's try together," he said with a smile.
They opened the clock carefully and found a tiny piece of sand inside. Faisal blew on it, and suddenly the clock began to tick! The boy jumped up and laughed.

"I'm Faisal," he said. "What's your name?" "Saad," answered the boy, and Faisal's heart beat fast, because Saad was his grandfather's name! "One day you'll have the best clock shop in Jeddah," Faisal said, and he turned the wheel forward.
Back in the shop, Grandpa was standing at the door with a big smile. "So, you met me," he said softly. "I waited sixty years to say thank you, Faisal."

pages.text: Every Friday morning, Faisal went fishing with his grandfather near the mangrove trees on the Red Sea coast. Grandfather always talked about the tall white herons that stood in the water. But this week he was quiet. "The herons have gone," he said sadly. "I don't know why."

After lunch, Faisal and his cousin Noura walked along the shore to look for clues. Under the mangrove trees, they found a terrible surprise. The roots were full of plastic bags, bottles and old fishing nets.
"Look!" said Noura. "The small fish can't swim between the roots now." Faisal thought for a moment. "And if there are no fish, the herons have no food," he said. "That's why they left!"

"We can't clean all this by ourselves," said Noura. So Faisal took photos with Grandfather's phone. The next day, he showed them to his class. Their teacher, Mr. Khalid, looked at the photos carefully and said, "Then we must help."

On Saturday, thirty students and their parents came to the beach with gloves and big bags. The sun was hot, but everyone worked hard until noon. Grandfather brought dates and cold water for all the helpers. By the end of the day, they had collected more than two hundred bags of rubbish!

A few weeks later, Faisal and Grandfather went back early in the morning. The water between the roots was clean now, and silver fish were moving quickly through it. Suddenly, Faisal saw something white and still. It was a heron, standing on one long leg.

Grandfather smiled the biggest smile Faisal had ever seen. "You brought the herons back," he said. "No, Grandfather," said Faisal. "We just gave them their home back." Now the class cleans the beach every month, and Faisal always carries a cloth bag instead of a plastic one.

stories.title: The Falcon at the Bus Stop

pages.text: It was a hot afternoon in Taif. Hamad was walking home from school when he heard a strange sound. Above the bus stop, a large bird was sitting on a lamp post. It was a falcon, and it looked very tired.
"Don't touch it!" shouted his friend Saleh. "It has sharp claws!" Hamad didn't want to touch it. He took out his water bottle and poured some water into the lid of his lunchbox.
Slowly, the falcon flew down and drank. Then Hamad saw a small silver ring on its leg. There was a phone number on the ring!

Hamad ran to the shop across the street and asked Uncle Mansour, the shopkeeper, to call the number. An old man answered, and his voice was shaking. "My falcon, Barq! I've looked for her for three days!"
Twenty minutes later, an old car stopped next to the bus stop. A man with a white beard got out and held up his arm. Barq flew straight to him, and the man smiled like a happy child.
"Thank you, my son," he said, and he took some money out of his pocket. Hamad shook his head politely. "No, thank you, sir. My grandfather always says kindness is free."
The old man laughed. "Your grandfather is a wise man. Then let me give you something free, too." Every weekend after that, Hamad visited the old man's farm and learned how to look after falcons.

options: He saw a phone number on a ring on its leg

options: clever and good at knowing what is right

options: He was very emotional because he had lost his falcon for three days

questions.q: What was the "free" present the old man gave Hamad?
options: Lessons about falcons on his farm

pages.text: Every winter, Faisal's family went camping in the desert. This year, Grandpa brought a baby camel called Ward. Faisal and his sister Noura loved her soft brown hair and her big dark eyes.
After dinner, Grandpa pointed at the sky. "Look at that bright star," he said. "It is always in the north. Long ago, travellers used it to find their way home."

The next morning, Noura shouted, "Ward isn't here!" Her rope was on the ground, and small footprints went over the dunes. "Let's follow them," said Faisal, and they took some water, a torch and Grandpa's whistle.
They walked for a long time. The footprints went up and down the hills of sand. Then a strong wind started to blow, and the footprints began to disappear.
"I'm scared," said Noura, and Faisal held her hand. Suddenly, they heard a quiet cry behind a big rock. It was Ward, and her leg was caught in an old fence!

Faisal freed her leg carefully, but now it was evening and the camp was far away. He looked up and saw the bright star. "This morning we walked north," he said. "So our camp is south, and we must keep the star behind us."

After an hour, they saw a small orange fire. Faisal blew the whistle, and Grandpa ran to meet them. "You found Ward, and you found your way home!" he said with a big smile. That night, they all sat by the fire and looked up at their star.

options: Because a strong wind started to blow

questions.q: What does "scared" mean in the story?

options: At the top of a tree

options: He remembered Grandpa's lesson about the star

pages.text: Every winter, Omar visited his grandfather's farm in the desert. Grandpa had twenty camels, but Omar's favourite was a baby camel called Noor. She had soft white hair and big brown eyes.
One evening, a strong wind started to blow. Sand flew everywhere, and the sky turned orange. "Quick, Omar! Help me bring the camels inside the fence!" shouted Grandpa.
When the wind stopped, Grandpa counted the camels. "Nineteen," he said quietly. "Noor is missing." Her mother, Zahra, walked up and down the fence and cried loudly.
Omar and Grandpa took a torch and drove slowly into the dark desert. They looked behind rocks and bushes, but they couldn't find her. "The desert is very big," said Grandpa. "We need a better idea."
Then Omar had one. "Zahra can find her baby! Camels can hear and smell very well." Grandpa smiled and opened the gate. Zahra ran into the night, and they followed her with the torch.
After twenty minutes, Zahra stopped near a small hill and made a long, low sound. A tiny voice answered from behind the hill. There was Noor, tired and covered in sand, but safe!
Back at the farm, Omar sat next to the fence and watched Noor sleeping beside her mother. "You were very clever tonight," said Grandpa. Omar laughed. "No, Grandpa, Zahra was the clever one!"

options: Not in its place and cannot be found

options: Because Zahra could run faster than the car
Because camels can hear and smell very well
Because Zahra could see in the dark

options: Because Zahra found Noor, not Omar

stories.title: The Star That Showed the Way

pages.text: Last winter, Sara and her grandfather drove into the desert to watch the stars. They put up a small tent next to their car. "There are no city lights here, so the sky is darker," Grandpa said.
Sara opened a space app on her phone. "Look, Grandpa! The app shows the names of all the planets and stars." Grandpa smiled. "My father taught me the stars without a phone," he said.

Later, they walked up a big sand hill and saw a bright light moving across the sky. "That's the space station!" Sara shouted. "Astronauts live and work up there." They watched it until it disappeared.
When they turned around, they couldn't see the car or the tent. Every hill looked the same in the dark. Sara looked at her phone, but the battery was empty. "Grandpa, we're lost!" she said quietly.
"Don't worry," Grandpa said calmly. He pointed to a small star in the north. "That star never moves. Our camp is south of this hill, so we must walk away from it."
They walked slowly with the star behind them. Sara counted her steps and listened to the wind. After a few minutes, she saw the shape of their car in the moonlight.

Back at the tent, Grandpa made hot tea, and Sara wrapped herself in a warm blanket. "Tomorrow night, can you teach me more stars?" she asked. "Of course," Grandpa laughed. "Your phone can sleep, but the stars never do."

pages.text: Yusuf was new at school in AlUla. He was quiet, and he didn't play football with the other boys at break time. After school, he helped his grandfather on their date farm. His job was to catch the falling dates before they hit the ground.
One morning, Coach Hamad looked worried. "Our goalkeeper, Majed, is ill," he said. "The final is on Thursday, and we don't have another goalkeeper." Nobody wanted the job.
Yusuf put up his hand slowly and said, "I can try." Some boys laughed. "You never play football!" said Turki. But the coach smiled and gave Yusuf a pair of goalkeeper gloves.

On Thursday, the stadium was full of families. Yusuf's grandfather sat in the front row with a bag of dates. The other team was bigger and faster, but Yusuf caught every ball. The score was one-one at the end of the match.
Then it was time for penalties. Both teams scored four goals. The last player from the other team ran towards the ball and kicked it very hard. Yusuf watched the ball carefully, like a falling date.
He jumped high to the left and caught it with both hands! Now Turki had to take the last kick for Yusuf's team. He scored, and everyone shouted, "We won!"

After the match, Turki shook Yusuf's hand and said sorry for laughing. "Where did you learn to catch like that?" he asked. Yusuf smiled at his grandfather in the front row. "On our date farm," he said, "and dates are much smaller than footballs!"

pages.text: Every summer, Faisal and his sister Layla visited their grandfather's farm in Taif. His pink roses were famous, and he made rose water from them. But this summer, Grandpa looked worried. "Someone is taking my roses," he said. "Every morning, more flowers are missing!"

"Let's be detectives!" said Layla. Faisal took his notebook and a torch, and they went to the garden. Near the roses, they found three clues: pink petals on the ground, strange round marks in the soil, and a small hole under the fence.

"A thief can't get through that small hole," said Faisal. "Maybe it's a goat?" "No," said Layla. "A goat eats leaves too, but all the leaves are still here." Faisal wrote everything carefully in his notebook.
That night, the children hid behind the big water tank with Grandpa. The moon was bright, and the garden was very quiet. They waited and waited. Then Layla whispered, "Look! Something is moving!"
Something round and slow came through the hole under the fence. Faisal turned on his torch. It was a tortoise! It walked to the roses and happily started eating the pink petals.

The next morning, they saw a poster on the neighbour's gate: "LOST: Our tortoise, Sultan. Please call Hamad." The children carried the tortoise next door, and little Hamad hugged his pet. "Sultan loves flowers," he said. "I'm so sorry!"

Hamad's father fixed the hole in the fence, and Grandpa's roses were safe again. A week later, Grandpa gave Hamad a small bottle of rose water and one pink rose. "The rose is for Sultan," he laughed. Faisal closed his notebook and smiled. "Mystery solved!"

options: He wasn't angry anymore and wanted to be kind

pages.text: Rayan and Majed were best friends, but a wide, busy road was between their buildings. They couldn't cross it alone. So they made a secret code with small mirrors. Every evening at sunset, they sent flashes of light from their balconies.
One flash meant "Hello!" Two flashes meant "I finished my homework." Three quick flashes meant "Let's meet at the park tomorrow!" Their mothers laughed and called them "the lighthouse boys."
But one evening, Majed's balcony stayed dark. Rayan waited and waited until the sky turned purple. "Maybe he forgot," said his sister Lama. But Rayan felt worried.
The next evening, there was still no light. At school, Majed's chair was empty too. "Majed has a high fever," the teacher said, "so he must stay in bed this week."

After school, Rayan had an idea and asked his father, "Can we visit Majed with something special?" His father smiled and drove him across the road. Rayan carried a small box and a bag of his grandmother's soft dates.

Majed was pale and tired, but his eyes became bright when he saw his friend. Rayan opened the box, and inside was a small torch. "Now you don't need the sun," Rayan said. "You can send me light from your bed!"

That night, Rayan stood on his balcony and looked at Majed's window. Suddenly, a tiny light flashed: once, twice, three times, four times! They didn't have a code for four flashes, but Rayan understood it perfectly. It meant "Thank you, my friend."

pages.text: Sara and her little brother Omar were camping with their family in the desert near Riyadh. The sand was hot and golden, and there were no trees anywhere. Omar looked at the empty land and asked, "Is there any water under all this sand?"
"Let's find out," said Sara with a smile. "Our science teacher showed us an experiment last week. We only need a hole, a cup, some plastic and a small stone."
Together they dug a deep hole and put the cup in the middle of it. Then they covered the hole with the plastic and put the stone on top, right above the cup. "Now we wait for the sun," Sara said.
All afternoon, the sun shone on the plastic. Omar checked it every hour. "Nothing is happening!" he said. But under the plastic, tiny drops of water were starting to appear.

The hot sun warmed the sand, and a little water from deep inside it went up into the air. When the water touched the cool plastic, it changed back into drops. Slowly, the drops ran down to the stone and fell into the cup.
In the evening, Father lifted the plastic carefully. There was a little water at the bottom of the cup! "It's only a few drops, but it came from dry sand!" Omar shouted happily.

That night, the family sat under the bright stars and drank sweet tea. Grandfather smiled and said, "Long ago, travellers in the desert knew that water hides in surprising places." Sara and Omar decided to show their experiment at the school science fair.

options: Because it touched the cool plastic

pages.text: Every winter, Faisal and his sister Reem visited their grandfather's camp in the desert. At night, Grandpa showed them the sky. "Look at that bright star," he said. "It is always in the north, so it can help you find your way home."

The next morning, Grandpa's baby camel, Noor, was missing. "She was hungry, and she walked away to find plants," Grandpa said sadly. Faisal looked at the sand and saw small footprints. "We can follow her tracks!" he shouted.

Grandpa took a torch and some water bottles, and they all walked north between the high sand dunes. The sun was very hot, and the wind was getting stronger. "Hurry," said Reem. "The wind is going to cover the tracks."
Near some big rocks, they heard a quiet sound. Noor was lying in the shade, and her leg was stuck between two stones. Faisal moved the stones carefully, and the little camel stood up.

But when they turned around, the tracks were gone. "The wind covered everything!" Reem said. Then the sun went down, and the desert became dark and cold. Grandpa smiled and asked, "Faisal, do you remember last night?"
Faisal looked up and found the bright star. "We walked north this morning, so now we must walk away from the star," he said. They walked slowly under the moon, and Noor followed them.

After an hour, they saw the orange fire of the camp. Grandma was waiting with hot tea and dates, and Noor ran to her mother. "You found the way home," Grandpa said proudly. "Tomorrow night, I am going to teach you more stars."

pages.text: Faisal's family bought a new robot cleaner. It was round, quiet and very fast. His little sister Noura called it "Mr. Zoom."
On the first day, Mr. Zoom cleaned the kitchen floor perfectly. But then strange things started to happen. First, Dad's sock disappeared. Then Mum's pen disappeared, and then the TV remote!
"Someone in this house is a thief!" said Dad. Everyone looked at the cat, Simsim. Simsim looked back at them and yawned.
That evening, Grandpa came to visit. After dinner, he looked everywhere. "Where are my glasses?" he asked. "I put them down next to my chair, and now I can't read my newspaper!"
Suddenly, Faisal had an idea. He lay on the floor and looked under the big sofa. It was very dark, but he could see something shiny.

He pulled out Dad's sock, Mum's pen, the remote, three coins, a toy car and Grandpa's glasses. At the back, Mr. Zoom was sitting quietly, like a dragon with its treasure. Noura laughed so much that she fell off her chair!

Grandpa put on his glasses and smiled at the robot. "What a clever machine!" he said. "But next time, please clean the floor and don't steal our things!" The next day, Simsim sat on top of Mr. Zoom and rode around the house like a king.

pages.text: Every Friday morning, Layla and her grandfather took his small blue boat out on the Red Sea. The water near the Farasan Islands was clear and green, and Layla could see the coral below. "The sea is like a big book," Grandpa said. "You must learn to read it."

That morning, Layla saw something strange near the rocks. A sea turtle was moving very slowly, and an old fishing net was wrapped around its front leg. "It can't swim properly," Layla said. "Grandpa, we have to help it!"

Grandpa stopped the engine and took out his small knife. "Hold the net, but be gentle," he said. "Turtles are stronger than they look." Layla's hands were shaking, but she held the net carefully while Grandpa cut it, one piece at a time.

At last, the turtle was free. Before it swam away, Layla noticed a white mark on its shell, shaped like a little star. "I'll call you Najma," she whispered, because Najma means star. The turtle looked at her for a moment, then dived into the deep blue water.
Months passed, and Layla often thought about Najma. Then, one warm summer night, Grandpa woke her up. "Come quietly," he said. "And don't turn on any lights."

They walked down to the beach under the moon. A big turtle was slowly digging a hole in the sand. When the moonlight shone on its shell, Layla saw a small white star. "Najma!" she said softly. "She came back!"

Najma laid her eggs, covered them with sand, and walked back into the sea. Grandpa smiled at Layla. "You read the sea very well," he said. "Because you helped her, there will be many new turtles in our ocean."

pages.text: Every summer in Riyadh, the afternoons were very hot. Sami's school had an invention fair next week, but he had no ideas. "Everyone is making a robot or a machine," he said to his sister Huda. "I want to make something different."
That afternoon, Sami saw a small bird on the balcony. It was drinking from a metal bowl, but the water was as hot as tea. The bird flew away quickly. "Poor bird," said Huda. "It's still thirsty."

In the evening, they visited Grandpa. He gave them water from an old clay jar, and it was surprisingly cold. "How is this water so cool without a fridge?" Sami asked. "The outside of the jar is wet," Grandpa smiled. "When that water goes into the air, the jar becomes cooler."

Suddenly, Sami had an idea. He and Huda put a small clay pot inside a bigger one, with wet sand between them. On top, they made a little roof from palm leaves to give shade. "It's a cool drink for birds," Sami said proudly.
The next day, they put their invention on the balcony and waited. For a long time, nothing happened. Then a sparrow landed on the edge, then another, then three more. "They love it!" Huda whispered.

At the fair, other students showed flying drones and talking robots. Sami felt nervous about his pots and sand. But the judges listened carefully, and one teacher touched the water. "It's cold!" she said. "And it doesn't need any electricity."

Sami didn't win first prize, but he won the prize for the best idea for nature. Soon, many families in their street made bird coolers too. Every afternoon, Grandpa sat on the balcony and counted the birds. "Old ideas can make new inventions," he said.

pages.text: Sara looked out of the big train window. "How long is the journey to Hail, Grandpa?" she asked. "About six hours," Grandpa said with a smile. "When I was young, it took twelve days."

Grandpa took an old brown notebook out of his bag. "I travelled this way by camel with my father," he said. "I wrote everything in here." The pages were yellow, and there were small drawings of tents, wells and stars.

Sara read one page aloud: "Today we passed a rock that looks like a sleeping camel. Father says it means we are halfway." "Can we see that rock from the train?" Sara asked. "Maybe," said Grandpa. "Keep your eyes open."
For two hours, Sara watched the desert. She saw sand, small hills and a family of camels near a road, but no sleeping camel. Grandpa closed his eyes. "Wake me if you find it," he said quietly.
Then, suddenly, Sara saw it. A long red rock was lying in the sand, with a round head and a hump on its back. "Grandpa! Wake up! It's the sleeping camel!" she shouted.
Grandpa opened his eyes and looked for a long time. "Sixty years," he whispered. "It hasn't changed at all." Other passengers came to the window too, and a little boy laughed and waved at the rock.

Grandpa gave Sara the notebook and a pencil. "Now it's your turn to write," he said. Sara thought for a moment. Then she wrote on a new page: "Today I passed the sleeping camel with Grandpa. We are halfway, and the best part of the journey is still ahead."

pages.text: The sun was hot over the school field in Jeddah. Today was Sports Day, and Faisal's team was in the big relay race. There were four boys on each team, and each boy had to run one part of the track.
Faisal was the fastest runner, so he was going to run last. "Don't worry," he told his friend Omar. "Just hold the baton tightly and give it to me." Omar nodded, but his hands were shaking.
The teacher blew his whistle, and the race started. Khalid ran first, then Sami, and they were winning! Now Sami was passing the baton to Omar.
Omar took the baton and started running. But halfway around the track, it fell from his hand and rolled across the grass. The other runners went past him, and the crowd shouted, "Oh no!"
Omar stopped and looked at Faisal with sad eyes. "Pick it up, Omar!" Faisal called. "You can do it! The race isn't finished!"
Omar picked up the baton and ran as fast as he could. When Faisal took it, his team was last. Faisal ran like the wind and passed one boy, then another, then another!

Faisal crossed the finish line just behind the winner, and his team came second. "Thank you for not getting angry," Omar said with a big smile. Faisal laughed and put his arm around him. "We're a team, Omar. Next year, we'll win together!"

pages.text: Omar lived with his grandfather near a big date farm in Al-Ahsa. Grandfather's back often hurt, so Omar built a small robot from old parts. He called it Tamr, because it was brown like a date.

Tamr was slow, and its arms were very short. "This robot can't even climb a tree!" laughed Omar's cousin Khalid. Omar felt sad, but Grandfather smiled. "Wait and see. Every helper is good at something."

Tamr couldn't climb, but it had big ears and a bright light on its head. It could hear very quiet sounds, and it could carry heavy baskets on its back. Every afternoon, it carried dates from the trees to the house.

One evening, the sky turned orange and a strong wind started to blow. "A sandstorm is coming!" shouted Grandfather. Everyone ran inside, but then Khalid noticed that his little goat, Snowy, was missing.
Outside, nobody could see anything because of the sand. Then Tamr's ears moved. "I can hear something," it said in its funny metal voice, and it rolled slowly into the storm.
Omar waited by the window with his heart beating fast. After ten long minutes, a small light appeared between the palm trees. It was Tamr, and Snowy was sitting safely in the basket on its back!

Khalid hugged his goat and looked at the robot. "I'm sorry, Tamr. You're the best helper on the farm." Grandfather laughed and said, "You see? Short arms, but a big heart." That night, Omar put a new sticker on Tamr. It said: Hero.

pages.text: Omar and his sister Noura sat in the back of the car. Outside, the desert was gold and orange, and big rocks stood like giants. "We're going to visit Hegra," said Dad. "People lived here more than two thousand years ago, and their history belongs to everyone."

At Hegra, the old tombs were cut into huge rocks, and each one had a tall door with beautiful shapes above it. "How did they make these without machines?" asked Noura. "With simple tools, lots of time and strong hands," said the guide, Mr. Saleh.

Mr. Saleh showed them some old writing on a wall. "The Nabataeans wrote this," he explained. "They were traders, and their camels carried spices and perfume across the desert." Omar closed his eyes and imagined long lines of camels under the stars.

While the others were walking to the next tomb, Omar saw something shiny in the sand. He knelt down and brushed it carefully with his fingers. It was a small, round coin with a face on it! "Noura, look!" he whispered.
Noura's eyes grew wide. "Is it treasure? Can we keep it?" she asked. Omar wanted to put it in his pocket. But then he remembered Dad's words: "History belongs to everyone."

Omar ran to Mr. Saleh and opened his hand. The guide looked at the coin for a long time. "This is a Nabataean coin, and it's very old and important," he said quietly. "Thank you for being honest, Omar."

A few months later, a letter arrived from the museum. Inside, there was a photo of the coin in a glass case, with a small card under it: Found by Omar, age ten. Omar smiled proudly and said, "Now everyone can see it."
